rows.question: What went wrong at Cloudflare?
rows.reference_answer: . A bad config (router rule) caused all of their edge routers to crash, taking down all of Cloudflare.
rows.answer: Cloudflare has experienced multiple distinct incidents involving power losses, routing errors, software bugs, and configuration mistakes [E1][E2][E3][E4][E5][E6][E7][E8][E9][E10]. _(unverified)_ Incorrectly set breaker coordination settings at the Portland data center caused a complete power loss [E1]. An incorrect ordering of disabled BGP advertised prefixes caused malfunctions across 19 datacenters [E2]. A partial switch misbehavior triggered a cascading Byzantine failure impacting API and dashboard availability for six hours and 33 minutes [E3]. A Tiered Cache system change caused status code 530 request failures for nearly six hours [E4]. On January 24, 2023, a code release error for service tokens made several services unavailable for 121 minutes [E5]. On October 4, 2023, DNS resolution problems caused SERVFAIL responses from 07:00 to 11:00 UTC [E6]. A dashboard React component bug caused excessive API calls and broader failures [E7]. On November 18, 2025, a database permission change in bot-detection systems propagated an oversized file, causing a systemwide outage [E8]. _(unverified)_ A bad router rule config crashed all edge routers [E9], and human error during abuse remediation mistakenly disabled the R2 Gateway service [E10].

monitored during mitigation and the team validated recovery against normal error rates before closing the
incident. Support staff linked customer tickets to this incident record. Follow-up actions include reviewing
alerts, updating escalation contacts, and verifying rollback procedures during the next scheduled exercise.
The final review is the authoritative source for revised causal conclusions and downstream service impact.
## Response record
The duty manager retained this preliminary report for audit.

decisions separate from unverified hypotheses. Each handover named the next check, its expected signal,
and the engineer responsible for reporting the result.

mitigation and compared it with the next ten-minute window. Changes were applied to one instance first,
with a second engineer checking rollback readiness and watching saturation.
For response record, Mira Chen reviewed sample window 3. Support collected representative request
identifiers and removed account details before sharing the examples. Responders used those identifiers to
align application traces with database activity without exposing customer information.
## Operational evidence
The diagnostic sample showed p95 latency of 840 ms and a 2.1% retry rate.

The April 1958 Florida tornado outbreak was a severe weather event that primarily affected the Florida peninsula on April 15, 1958.
 A total of five tornadoes touched down in the state of Georgia between 12–5 p.m. EST.
 80 percent of the tornadoes were recorded in Florida, while 75 percent of the Florida events attained F3 intensity or greater.
 The strongest tornado produced F4 damage on the Fujita scale in Polk County, Florida, becoming one of only two F4 tornadoes recorded in the U.S. state of Florida.
 The second F4 tornado occurred on April 4, 1966, in Polk County near Gibsonia and Galloway.
 In total, 65–72 people were injured during the 1958 outbreak, but no deaths were directly related to the tornadoes.
 In addition to confirmed tornadoes, an unconfirmed tornado was also reported near Wimauma, Florida.

In North America, a bowl game is one of a number of post-season college football games that are primarily played by teams belonging to the NCAA's Division I Football Bowl Subdivision (FBS).
 Prior to 2002, bowl game statistics were not included in players' career totals and the games were mostly considered to be exhibition games involving a payout to participating teams.

 The increase in bowl games has necessitated the steady easing of the NCAA bowl eligibility rules since 2006, as teams with a losing record are often required to fill some of the 78 available bowl slots.

rows.question: What went wrong at CircleCI?
rows.reference_answer: . A deploy changed the type of a field in the PostgreSQL database used by the job-distribution service. Newly-written rows used the new type and old rows used the old type, so the distributor's strict schema validation failed on each scan and it stopped distributing work. Rolling back made the rows written between the two deploys unreadable, so distribution kept failing; recovery required hand-deploying a build that ignored the offending field, plus manual scaling.

## reporting-api
The reporting-api service depends on ledger-service. Data Products maintains its deployment and capacity budget. The availability objective is 99.9% over a rolling thirty-day window. Inbound requests carry correlation identifiers; durable events leave through the outbox. Consumers acknowledge only after persistence and use idempotency keys when replaying work. Journal events update a read projection that serves merchant dashboards. The projection stores both a processing checkpoint and a last-refresh timestamp. Requests return the checkpoint with the report so support can distinguish stale data from missing writes. Rebuilding the projection runs alongside the active view and switches readers only after row counts and aggregate balances agree.

Northwind Pay INC-2020 (2025-02-17). Authentication retries. The affected services were auth-service.
Causal analysis remains in the final review. Responders recorded the incident timeline in the operations
channel and preserved application logs for later analysis. The on-call engineer coordinated service health
checks with the infrastructure team. Traffic was monitored during mitigation and the team validated recovery
against normal error rates before closing the incident. Support staff linked customer tickets to this incident
record. Follow-up actions include reviewing alerts, updating escalation contacts, and verifying rollback
procedures during the next scheduled exercise. The final review is the authoritative source for revised
causal conclusions and downstream service impact.
## Response record
The duty manager retained this preliminary report for audit.
For response record, Sam Okafor reviewed sample window 1. The responder compared the primary
dashboard with an independent probe before changing traffic. A healthy aggregate can hide a single tenant
with repeated failures, so the investigation retained tenant-level samples.
For response record, Nadia Patel reviewed sample window 2. The team checked queue age as well as
queue depth because a small backlog can still contain old work. Successful processing was verified against
durable records rather than inferred from a green worker heartbeat.
For response record, Nadia Patel reviewed sample window 3. The responder compared the primary
dashboard with an independent probe before changing traffic. A healthy aggregate can hide a single tenant
with repeated failures, so the investigation retained tenant-level samples.
## Operational evidence
The diagnostic sample showed p95 latency of 840 ms and a 2.1% retry rate.
